chapter_approach.heading: How this chapter is taught
chapter_approach.intro: The chapter follows the book's own order: smaller units first, then tenths and hundredths as parts of a unit, then the decimal point as a way of writing them, then comparing and computing. Every decimal rule is reached from the fractions the student already knows.

points.title: Try first, name later

points.title: Fractions underneath every decimal
points.text: A decimal is a count of tenths, hundredths or thousandths. Adding, subtracting and comparing decimals use the same place value moves as whole numbers, so nothing is a trick to remember.

points.title: One zoom per digit
points.text: On the number line each digit names one more zoom into ten equal parts, and the end marks of a line decide what one division is worth.

points.title: Concept, then practice, topic by topic
points.text: Each idea gets its own topic with one video per concept and a practice concept at the end; interactive tools appear only where handling the numbers is the idea. The book's questions follow in their own topic, one question and one video per concept.

content.text:
3.1 The Need for Smaller Units
Sonu's mother was fixing a toy. She was trying to join two pieces with the help of a screw. Sonu was watching his mother with great curiosity. His mother was unable to join the pieces. Sonu asked why. His mother said that the screw was not of the right size.
She brought another screw from the box and was able to fix the toy.
The two screws looked the same to Sonu. But when he observed them closely, he saw they were of slightly different lengths.
Sonu was fascinated by how such a small difference in lengths could matter so much. He was curious to know the difference in lengths. He was also curious to know how little the difference was because the screws looked nearly the same.

Worked example: A ruler has every centimetre split into 10 equal parts. One screw ends 7 parts after the 2 cm mark and another ends 2 parts after the 3 cm mark. Write each length and say what the first one means.
1. The first screw is more than 2 1/2 cm but less than 3 cm, so it lies between 2 cm and 3 cm.
2. The unit between two consecutive numbers is divided into 10 equal parts, so each part is 1/10 cm.
3. From 0 we go to 2, then take 7 parts of 1/10: the length is 2 cm and 7/10 cm, that is 2 7/10 cm.
4. In the same way the second screw is 3 cm and 2/10 cm, that is 3 2/10 cm.
Answer: First screw 2 7/10 cm, second screw 3 2/10 cm

3.2 A Tenth Part
The length of the pencil shown in the figure below is 3 4/10 units, which can also be read as 3 units and four one-tenths, i.e., (3 × 1) + (4 × 1/10) units.
10 times 1/10 is 1 unit. This length is the same as 34 one-tenths units because 10 one-tenths units make one unit.
34 × 1/10 = 34/10 = 10/10 + 10/10 + 10/10 + 4/10 (34 one-tenths) = 1 + 1 + 1 + 4/10 (3 and 4 one-tenths).

Worked example: A pencil is 3 4/10 units long. Write its length as a count of tenths and show why it is the same length.
1. 10 one-tenths make 1 unit, so 3 units is 3 × 10 = 30 tenths.
2. 30 tenths and 4 tenths make 34 tenths, so the length is 34/10 units.
3. Check: 34/10 = 10/10 + 10/10 + 10/10 + 4/10, and each 10/10 is 1 unit, so that is 1 + 1 + 1 + 4/10 = 3 4/10.
Answer: 34/10 units

content.text:
Sonu is measuring some of his body parts. The length of Sonu's lower arm is 2 7/10 units, and that of his upper arm is 3 6/10 units. What is the total length of his arm?
To get the total length, let us see the lower and upper arm length as 2 units and 7 one-tenths, and 3 units and 6 one-tenths, respectively. So, there are (2 + 3) units and (7 + 6) one-tenths. Together, they make 5 units and 13 one-tenths. But 13 one-tenths is 1 unit and 3 one-tenths. So, the total length is 6 units and 3 one-tenths.
(2 + 3) + (7/10 + 6/10) = (2 + 3) + (13/10) = 5 + 13/10 = 5 + 10/10 + 3/10 = 5 + 1 + 3/10 = 6 + 3/10 = 6 3/10.
Or, both the lengths can be converted to tenths and then added: 27 one-tenths and 36 one-tenths is 63 one-tenths, 27/10 + 36/10 = 63/10. 63/10 is the same as 60 one-tenths (60/10) and 3 one-tenths (3/10), which is equal to 6 units and 3 one-tenths, i.e., 6 3/10.

content.text:
The length of Shylaja's hand is 12 4/10 units, and her palm is 6 7/10 units, as shown in the picture. What is the length of the longest (middle) finger?
The length of the finger can be found by evaluating (12 + 4/10) − (6 + 7/10). This can be done in different ways. For example, (a) 12 + 4/10 − 6 − 7/10 = (12 − 6) + (4/10 − 7/10) = 6 − 3/10 = 5 + 1 − 3/10 = 5 + 10/10 − 3/10 = 5 + 7/10 = 5 7/10. Discuss what is being done here and why.
(b) As in the case of counting numbers, it is convenient to start subtraction from the tenths. We cannot remove 7 one-tenths from 4 one-tenths. So we split a unit from 12 and convert it to 10 one-tenths. Now, the number has 11 units and 14 one-tenths. We subtract 7 one-tenths from 14 one-tenths and then subtract 6 units from 11 units. 12 4/10 becomes 11 14/10, and 11 14/10 − 6 7/10 = 5 7/10.

interaction_points.prompt: What are the next four numbers?

video_script.why: The child can add and subtract numbers with tenths and now uses the difference of two neighbours to continue six patterns.
video_script.substitution: Take the earlier number from the later one to find the change, then add or take away that change four more times.
video_script.anchor: Six number patterns written in rows, each with two or three numbers shown and four empty boxes after them
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko reads the change in the first pattern as the digit 3 and adds 3 instead of 3 tenths, but 4 to 4 3/10 grows by only 3 tenths.
video_script.payoff_line: The first pattern goes on to four and nine tenths, then five and two tenths

final_answer.spoken: the first pattern goes on to four and nine tenths, five and two tenths, five and five tenths, and five and eight tenths

maths_rules: Pattern 4: 5 3/10 is 4/10 less than 5 7/10, take away 4/10 each time: 4 9/10, 4 5/10, 4 1/10, 3 7/10.
Pattern 5: 13 is 5/10 less than 13 5/10, take away 5/10 each time: 12, 11 5/10, 11, 10 5/10.
Pattern 6: 10 4/10 is 1 1/10 less than 11 5/10, take away 1 1/10 each time: 8 2/10, 7 1/10, 6, 4 9/10.
Slip: the change 3/10 is read as 3.
video_script.design: One idea: the change between two neighbours is used again and again. Assumes the child can add and subtract numbers with tenths. Wrong idea: read the tenths digit as a whole number. The six rows stay all video; the working band shows the changes and the answer beat fills the boxes. Most of the numbers are on the board and not spoken.

concepts.concept_name: Splitting a tenth into ten parts

content.text:
3.3 A Hundredth Part
The length of a sheet of paper was 8 9/10 units, which can also be said as 8 units and 9 one-tenths. It is folded in half along its length. What is its length now?
We can say that its length is between 4 4/10 units and 4 5/10 units. But we cannot state its exact measurement, since there are no markings. Earlier, we split a unit into 10 one-tenths to measure smaller lengths. We can do something similar and split each one-tenth into 10 parts.
What is the length of this smaller part? How many such smaller parts make a unit length?
As shown in the figure below, each one-tenth has 10 smaller parts, and there are 10 one-tenths in a unit; therefore, there will be 100 smaller parts in a unit. Therefore, one part's length will be 1/100 of a unit.
Returning to our question, what is the length of the folded paper? We can see that it ends at 4 4/10 5/100, read as 4 units and 4 one-tenths and 5 one-hundredths.
Math Talk: How many one-hundredths make one-tenth? Can we also say that the length is 4 units and 45 one-hundredths?

content.text:
Worked example: A paper strip 8 9/10 units long is folded in half. Its new length ends between 4 4/10 and 4 5/10. Split each tenth into 10 parts: what is one small part, and where does the folded strip end? Can the length also be said as 4 units and 45 hundredths?
1. Each tenth has 10 smaller parts and a unit has 10 tenths, so a unit has 10 × 10 = 100 smaller parts.
2. One part is 1/100 of a unit.
3. The folded strip ends 5 parts after the 4 4/10 mark, so it is 4 units and 4 tenths and 5 hundredths.
4. 10 hundredths make 1 tenth, so 4 tenths is 40 hundredths, and 40 + 5 = 45 hundredths.
5. So yes, the length is also 4 units and 45 hundredths, that is 4 45/100.
Answer: 4 4/10 5/100, which is also 4 45/100 units

maths_rules: 8 9/10 folded in half gives 4 4/10 5/100 = 4 45/100 units.

What will be the sum of 15 3/10 4/100 and 2 6/10 8/100? This can be solved in different ways. Some are shown below.
Method 1: (15 + 2) + (3/10 + 6/10) + (4/100 + 8/100) = 17 + 9/10 + 12/100 = 17 + 9/10 + 1/10 + 2/100 = 17 + 10/10 + 2/100 = 18 2/100. 10 hundredths is the same as 1 tenth.
Method 2: written as a column, the tenths add to 9 and the hundredths add to 12, which is 1 tenth and 2 hundredths, so 10 tenths, which is 1 unit, and 2 hundredths: 18 2/100.
Math Talk: Are both these methods different? Observe the addition done below for 483 + 268. Do you see any similarities between the methods shown above? (400 + 80 + 3) + (200 + 60 + 8) = (400 + 200) + (80 + 60) + (3 + 8) = 600 + 140 + 11 = 600 + 150 + 1 = 700 + 50 + 1 = 751.
One can also find the sum 15 3/10 4/100 + 2 6/10 8/100 by converting to hundredths, as follows. (c) (15 + 2) + (34/100 + 68/100) = 17 + 102/100 = 17 + 1 + 2/100 = 18 2/100. (d) 1534/100 + 268/100 = 1802/100 = 1800/100 + 2/100 = 18 2/100.
100 hundredths is same as 1 unit. 15 is the same as 1500 hundredths and 2 is the same as 200 hundredths.

Worked example: Add 15 3/10 4/100 and 2 6/10 8/100 by adding place by place, and compare with the addition 483 + 268.
1. Units: 15 + 2 = 17. Tenths: 3 + 6 = 9. Hundredths: 4 + 8 = 12.
2. 12 hundredths is 1 tenth and 2 hundredths, so the tenths become 9 + 1 = 10 tenths.
3. 10 tenths is 1 unit, so the units become 17 + 1 = 18, leaving 2 hundredths: 18 2/100.
4. In 483 + 268 the ones add to 11, so one ten is carried; the tens add to 150, so one hundred is carried. It is the same carrying, with a different set of places.
Answer: 18 2/100

Worked example: Find 25 9/10 − 6 4/10 7/100, then check it by converting both numbers to hundredths.
1. There are no hundredths in 25 9/10 and 7 must be taken away, so break 1 tenth into 10 hundredths.
2. 25 9/10 becomes 25 8/10 10/100.
3. Hundredths: 10 − 7 = 3. Tenths: 8 − 4 = 4. Units: 25 − 6 = 19. So the answer is 19 4/10 3/100.
4. Check in hundredths: 2590 − 647 = 1943, and 1943/100 = 19 43/100, which is 19 4/10 3/100.
Answer: 19 4/10 3/100
